title: The Choir of Old Chapel Road
premise: Dominic Winterbourne, an urban explorer obsessed with documenting the undocumented, discovers a network of tunnels beneath Old Chapel Road that appear on no survey — and inside them, evidence that his childhood imaginary friend, Wren, was never imaginary at all. When Wren appears on his porch, unchanged after thirty years, Dominic learns the tunnels were dug by the town's founding families to bury an injustice: a child, Eliza Marsh, walled up alive in 1897 so her family could inherit her share of the estate. The choir heard singing from the chapel at night is Eliza's memory, repeating, and every descendant who inherited that stolen money owes a debt. To end it, Dominic must descend before sunrise, return what was taken, and give Eliza's name back to the town's records — knowing the debt collectors will take a life in exchange if he fails. He survives by offering not blood but truth: he reads Eliza into the official record as dawn breaks, and the choir finally falls silent.
about_author: Orsen Thornbury is the pen name of a former county archivist who spent eleven years cataloguing unclaimed estates and probate disputes in rural New England. Their fiction draws on real property ledgers, and they maintain that the most frightening documents are the ones with missing pages.

chapters.title: The Survey That Isn't
chapters.summary: POV Dominic. Dominic maps storm drains beneath Old Chapel Road and finds a brick-lined tunnel absent from every survey, its walls scratched with tally marks and a child's handwriting: 'they will come for the singers.' His documentation ritual is established as prayer. Emotional beat: the thrill of discovery curdling into unease when his own measurements refuse to match on a second pass.

chapters.title: Wren on the Porch
chapters.summary: POV Dominic. At dusk, Dominic finds Wren — his childhood imaginary friend, a boy in a sailor collar — sitting on his porch steps, physically real and exactly as remembered. Wren says only, 'You found the door. Now they know you can see.' Neighbors' porch lights flicker off one by one down the street. Emotional beat: nostalgic joy collapsing into dread.

chapters.title: The Probate Box
chapters.summary: POV Dominic. Digging through county archives, Dominic finds the Marsh estate file of 1897: three heirs listed, but only two signatures on the final settlement, and a page torn out where the third should be. The archivist who helps him goes pale reading the names of the founding families — including 'Winterbourne.' Emotional beat: inheritance revealed as something rotten.

chapters.title: What the Choir Sings
chapters.summary: POV Wren. Through Wren's alien, timeless perception, we learn the truth: Eliza Marsh was walled into the chapel crypt by her aunts and uncles, and her memory became the singing the town hears at night. The descendants' wealth is the payment; the collectors are what the aunts invited in to keep Eliza quiet. Emotional beat: grief for a child the world erased.

chapters.title: Neighbors Who Owe
chapters.summary: POV Dominic. Dominic confronts the last living descendants on Old Chapel Road; each admits privately to hearing the choir, each has lost someone — a brother, a daughter — on the eve of an inheritance. One old woman begs him to stop digging: 'The ledger balances itself, boy. It always finds a way.' Emotional beat: complicity and cowardice across generations.

chapters.title: The Torn Page
chapters.summary: POV Dominic. Wren leads Dominic through the tunnel to the chapel crypt, where the missing probate page is embedded in the mortar like a relic — proof of Eliza's existence and her stolen share. The walls breathe. Tally marks on the brick now count down instead of up. Emotional beat: awe and horror fused; documentation becomes desecration.

chapters.title: They Come Collecting
chapters.summary: POV Dominic. Nightfall. The collectors — tall figures wearing the faces of the 1897 signatories — walk Old Chapel Road house to house, knocking politely. Dominic barricades himself in the chapel with the page while they take the old woman next door, whose family kept the largest share. Emotional beat: terror and guilt; justice outside any law is still justice.

chapters.title: Sunrise Clause
chapters.summary: POV Wren. Wren explains the rule he died protecting: the debt can be discharged only if Eliza's name is entered in the public record before dawn — a truth spoken where the town must hear it. But the collectors are already peeling the chapel doors open, and Wren confesses he was the first child they took to keep the secret. Emotional beat: sacrifice foreshadowed.

chapters.title: Reading of the Name
chapters.summary: POV Dominic. Climax. As the doors splinter, Dominic stands in the crypt and reads the torn page aloud — Eliza Marsh, heir, murdered for her inheritance — recording it on his camera, streaming it live, shouting it into the dark. The collectors freeze mid-step. The wall cracks open. Eliza's voice joins the choir one last time, then stops. Emotional beat: defiant, cathartic release.

chapters.title: Amended Record
chapters.summary: POV Dominic. Dawn. The Marsh estate is formally reopened; the descendants' fortunes dissolve into probate limbo, which feels like mercy compared to what almost came. Wren fades on the porch steps, finally allowed to be a memory that ends. Dominic files his survey — tunnels and all — with the county, and the archive stamps it received. Emotional beat: quiet restitution; memory made permanent.
